# Filtering by file type in ripgrep

A *file type* in ripgrep is just a name attached to one or more globs. `rust`
means `*.rs`; `c` means `*.[chH]`, `*.[chH].in` and `*.cats`. Instead of
retyping `-g '*.{c,h}'` on every search, you name the set once and reuse it.
ripgrep ships with just over 200 built-in type definitions, and a handful have
aliases — `py` and `python`, `md` and `markdown`, `ts` and `typescript`,
`bat` and `batch` — so you can spell them the way you think of them.

## `-t/--type`: search only these files

```
$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
$ rg 'fn run' -trust          # short form; the value attaches directly
```

Repeat the flag to widen the net — multiple `-t` flags are OR'd:

```
$ rg TODO -trust -tmd
```

The moment you pass a single `-t`, ripgrep switches into whitelist mode: a file
that matches no selected type is skipped. This is the flag's real value on a
large tree — you are not just filtering output, you are not opening the files
at all.

`--type=all` is a special value meaning "every type currently defined,
including ones you added on this command line." It is whitelist mode over
ripgrep's whole type table: recognized files get searched, unrecognized ones
don't. A shell script named `my-shell-script` with no extension isn't matched
by the `sh` globs, so `-tall` skips it.

If you name a type that doesn't exist, ripgrep errors out rather than quietly
matching nothing — a typo'd `-tpyton` fails loudly.

## `-T/--type-not`: skip these files

```
$ rg clap --type-not rust
$ rg clap -Trust
```

`-T` is the mirror image and also repeatable. The asymmetry worth knowing: `-t`
puts everything else out of scope, while a lone `-T` only removes the named
type and leaves everything else searchable as usual.

You can mix them. When a file matches globs from more than one selection, the
**last one on the command line wins**, so ordering is how you carve out
exceptions:

```
$ rg config -tall -Tjson       # every recognized type except JSON
```

`--type-not=all` is the inverse of `--type=all`: it searches only files ripgrep
*doesn't* recognize. That's a good way to find the strays — extensionless
scripts, odd config files — that your type-based searches have been missing.

## `--type-list`: see what a type actually covers

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
```

One type per line, name, then `: `, then its globs comma-separated; both the
list and each type's globs are sorted. Reach for this before you assume a type
covers what you think — `js` includes `*.vue`, `*.cjs` and `*.mjs`; `css`
includes `*.scss`; `json` includes `composer.lock`. `--type-list` also reflects
any `--type-add` and `--type-clear` flags in the same invocation, which makes
it the way to check a custom definition before searching with it.

## `--type-add`: define your own

The format is `NAME:GLOB`, one glob per flag, additive to whatever ripgrep
already defines for that name:

```
$ rg title --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' -tweb
$ rg title --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb        # same thing
```

Defining a type does not select it — you still need `-tweb`.

There is also an include directive that composes existing types:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' -tsrc PATTERN
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' --type-add 'src:*.foo' -tsrc PATTERN
```

Included types must already be defined by the time the flag is parsed, so put
your `--type-add 'wat:*.wat'` before the `--type-add 'combo:include:wat,py'`
that references it. Type names must be only Unicode letters or numbers — no
punctuation — and `all` is reserved.

The related `--type-clear NAME` wipes a type's globs entirely; you can add new
ones afterward, but `--type-clear rust -trust` with nothing added back is an
error, because `rust` no longer exists.

**None of this persists.** Type settings apply to one invocation only. To keep
a definition, use a shell alias or a config file pointed at by
`RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH`, one argument per line:

```
--type-add
web:*.{html,css,js}
```

## Things that will bite you

- **Type globs match the file name only, not the path.** `--type-add
  'foo:src/*.rs'` will never match. Use `-g` for path-shaped patterns.
- **Types lose to globs and to ignore files.** Precedence runs `--glob` first,
  then ignore rules, then types. A gitignored file stays unsearched no matter
  what `-t` you pass; add `-u`/`--no-ignore` if you want it back.
- **Explicit paths bypass filtering.** `rg -tpy foo main.rs` searches
  `main.rs`. Type filtering applies to files ripgrep discovers by walking, not
  to ones you hand it.
- **Types never apply to directories,** so `-t` doesn't prune the traversal —
  it prevents files from being read and searched.

## Quick reference

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `-tTYPE` | search only TYPE (repeatable; whitelist mode) |
| `-t all` | search only recognized types |
| `-TTYPE` | skip TYPE (repeatable) |
| `-T all` | search only unrecognized files |
| `--type-add 'N:GLOB'` | add a glob to type N |
| `--type-add 'N:include:A,B'` | build N from existing types |
| `--type-clear N` | drop N's globs |
| `--type-list` | print all types and their globs |
